title: Read the whole tracker from one repo tarball
description:
The factory reads the tracker one file at a time over GitHub's contents API: 1104 GET requests per plan pass. Serial, that is a 14-minute pass that outlives its own 3-minute publish slot. Concurrent, it is 403s.

ROOT CAUSE, measured rather than assumed. It is not concurrency. GitHub's documented secondary limit is 900 POINTS PER MINUTE for REST, where most GETs cost 1 point, and separately allows up to 100 concurrent requests. 1104 reads is 1104 points however they are paced, so serial-but-fast trips the same wall. Picking a smaller concurrency number was never the fix, and 0h9's claim that 16 was "chosen against GitHub's limits" was wrong.
https://docs.github.com/en/rest/using-the-rest-api/rate-limits-for-the-rest-api

Two other things I asserted and should not have: Cloudflare's subrequest ceiling was never in play (paid Workers allow 10,000 per invocation), and a GitHub App token would not help (5,000/hr either way outside GHEC, and the points budget is unchanged).

THE FIX: read the whole tracker from the repository tarball, in one request.

    GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/tarball/{sha}

302s to codeload, and only the api.github.com hop is rate-limited, so the whole read costs ONE point. In a Workflow isolate:

    fetch(tarball)                                   // follows the 302
      .body.pipeThrough(new DecompressionStream("gzip"))   // native, no flag
      -> streaming tar walk, keep only .tick/issues/*.json
      -> JSON.parse each

Nothing is materialized: entries that are not tracker records are skipped without being retained, so the isolate's 128 MB ceiling applies to the 2.2 MB of JSON we keep, not to the 49 MB archive.

MEASURED on pengelbrecht/ticks, three runs, V8 (node; the hot path uses only APIs Workers have, so it transfers):

    download            18 MB gz, 2.5 s
    archive streamed    49 MB, 4332 entries
    records kept        1104 of 1104, 2.24 MB
    parse CPU           136 / 137 / 137 ms      (vs a 30 s default CPU limit)
    heap                ~10 MB                  (vs 128 MB)

So: one point instead of 1104, and 137 ms of CPU instead of a pass that never finished.

WHY NOT THE ALTERNATIVES
- git/trees?recursive=1 + per-blob reads: the tree is one request, but the blobs are still ~1100 requests on a cold pass. Better, not enough.
- GraphQL aliased blob reads: batches to ~12 requests, but adds a second API surface, a cost/complexity budget to reason about, and an open question about fine-grained PAT scope. The tarball is one request and needs none of it.
- Cloning in the sandbox container: correct in the long run and what every comparable system does (actions/checkout, Codex cloud, Cursor, Sourcegraph gitserver all clone; only Dependabot uses contents-per-file, for ~20 known manifests). But it moves the reconciler's reads into the container, which is an architecture change, not a fix. Keep it as the direction; this ticket does not need it.
- ETag/If-None-Match on the contents API: helps re-reads, does nothing for the cold pass that is failing.

SCOPE
1. A streaming tar reader (~100 lines, no dependency; 512-byte headers, name at 0, octal size at 124, payload padded to 512).
2. A tracker snapshot read that takes one tarball and returns every tick record, behind the existing ContentsStore seam so tests keep their in-memory store.
3. TrackerClient.#all() uses it. 0h9's READ_CONCURRENCY comes out with it - it was a band-aid that traded a timeout for a throttle.
4. Carry GitHub's status, Retry-After and message body in read errors. That gap is why the 403 could not be diagnosed from the error alone, and it stays worth fixing whatever the read path is.

Supersedes 0h9. Found by performing u9h.
acceptance_criteria: A plan pass reads the tracker in one GitHub request and completes well inside the publish slot TTL, proven against the deployed factory; read errors carry GitHub's status, Retry-After and message
closed_reason: Landed via PR #22: the tracker is read from one repo tarball. Root cause was GitHub's 900-points-per-minute secondary limit, not concurrency; 1104 reads is 1104 points however paced. Measured: 1104/1104 records, 137ms parse CPU, ~10MB heap, one API point. Supersedes 0h9.
